messages.content: I want to develop tactile slip prediction that distinguishes an impending grasp slip from elastic deformation, even across unseen materials and sensor wear.

The central distinction is between a tactile change that signals a grasp is about to slip and one that reflects elastic deformation without slip. The aim is predictive: identify impending slip early enough to warn about it, rather than merely recognize slip once it has begun. That distinction must remain reliable on held-out materials and with worn sensors.
What performance targets should define success?

The predictor should identify slip at least 100 milliseconds ahead, with at least 90% recall and no more than a 5% false-positive rate. Those targets must be met on held-out materials and worn sensors, including in evaluation that contains deformation-only contacts matched for force.
Does the 100-millisecond requirement mean detecting a slip within 100 milliseconds after it starts?
No. It is an advance-warning requirement: the prediction should come at least 100 milliseconds before the slip. Detecting it after it starts would not satisfy that timing target.
And recall refers to how many impending slips get flagged?

Yes. A recall of at least 90% means the predictor should flag at least 90% of the impending slips being evaluated under the specified advance-warning requirement. A prediction that arrives too late does not supply the required 100-millisecond warning.
Why specify a false-positive limit as well?

Because flagging nearly every contact as an impending slip could produce high recall without making the distinction you want. The false-positive rate must be no more than 5%, so contacts that are not impending slips should rarely be flagged as such. The requirement matters especially for elastic deformation without slip.
So elastic deformation is not itself the event to predict?

Right. The target event is impending grasp slip. Elastic deformation is the competing explanation for a tactile change: the contact can deform without an impending slip. The predictor needs to distinguish those situations, not treat every deformation-related change as a slip warning.
Why call out deformation-only contacts matched for force?

They make the distinction more demanding. A deformation-only contact is a non-slip case, and matching it for force means force alone should not make the comparison trivial. The predictor still needs to avoid calling that contact an impending slip while meeting the recall and false-positive targets.
Is a prediction good enough if it works on familiar materials but not on held-out ones?

No. The goal explicitly includes unseen materials, and the performance targets are to be met on held-out materials. Success limited to materials already familiar to the predictor would not establish the requested performance under that condition.
How does sensor wear fit into the same goal?

Sensor wear is another condition across which the distinction must hold. The targets are not only for held-out materials; they must also be met with worn sensors. The node does not specify a degree or mechanism of wear, only that worn sensors are part of the required evaluation.
Could I state the objective as predicting tactile change?

That would be too broad. Both impending slip and elastic deformation can involve tactile change, while the objective is specifically to predict impending grasp slip and distinguish it from deformation without slip. Keeping that contrast explicit also explains why the false-positive limit matters.
Would it be accurate to say the predictor should be sensitive but not over-eager?

Yes, as an informal description. The precise requirements are at least 90% recall for slip predictions made at least 100 milliseconds ahead, alongside a false-positive rate of no more than 5%. It must meet those targets on held-out materials and worn sensors, with force-matched deformation-only contacts included.
Does meeting the numerical targets in an easy set of contacts cover the force-matched deformation cases?

Not by itself. The requirement explicitly includes deformation-only contacts matched for force. The stated performance targets need to hold in the evaluation that includes those contacts; performance on contacts that do not test that distinction would leave part of the goal unaddressed.
Do the requirements specify a particular tactile sensor design or prediction method?

No. They specify the capability, timing, performance thresholds, and conditions under which those thresholds must be met. They do not choose a sensor design, a model, a signal-processing method, or a training procedure.
Nor do they define a particular material list or an exact amount of sensor wear, correct?

Correct. The conditions are held-out materials and worn sensors, but no particular materials or wear levels are named. Those unspecified details should not be presented as established parts of the goal.
I want the wording to make clear that the prediction is made before slip, while a deforming contact need not be a slip warning.

You could phrase it this way: Develop tactile prediction of impending grasp slip that distinguishes slip from elastic deformation without slip across unseen materials and sensor wear. Predict slip at least 100 milliseconds ahead with at least 90% recall and no more than a 5% false-positive rate, meeting those targets on held-out materials and worn sensors, including deformation-only contacts matched for force.
If a contact deforms but does not slip, should it be treated as evidence that the predictor caught an impending slip?

No. In this goal, a deformation-only contact is precisely a case that should not be mistaken for an impending slip. Including force-matched examples of those contacts helps make clear that success requires the predictor to discriminate, not just respond to deformation or force-related tactile changes.
And if the warning comes before slip, but less than 100 milliseconds before it?

It would still fall short of the stated lead-time target. The requirement is at least 100 milliseconds ahead. The recall target is therefore meaningful in conjunction with that timing requirement, not as permission to count late warnings as meeting the goal.

For the slip-prediction goal, I propose training a force-conditioned tactile model using shear-drift and strain-recovery signals, matched-force deformation negatives, and wear augmentation for 120-ms slip forecasts.

That is a proposed training approach, not a claim of measured performance. The model would use force as context while learning from shear-drift and strain-recovery signals. Deformation-only contacts matched for force would serve as negative examples, and wear augmentation would be part of training. The intended output is a forecast of slip 120 milliseconds ahead.
What does force-conditioned mean here? Is force itself the slip signal?

Force-conditioned means the model interprets the tactile signals in the context of force. It does not mean that force alone is being proposed as the indicator of impending slip. That distinction matters because the deformation negatives are matched for force: the model is meant to learn to distinguish the cases even when force is similar.
Why use both shear-drift and strain-recovery signals?

The proposal names both as inputs for learning the distinction between impending slip and elastic deformation. Shear-drift concerns changes associated with shear over time, while strain recovery concerns how deformation relaxes or recovers. Including both lets the proposed model consider those aspects together; the proposal does not establish that either signal, alone or in combination, will prove sufficient.
Should I describe strain recovery as a guaranteed sign that there will be no slip?

No. The proposal is to use strain-recovery signals as information for the model, not to declare a universal rule about what they mean. The model would need to learn the distinction from the proposed training examples, and its ability to do so remains to be evaluated.
What exactly are the matched-force deformation negatives doing in training?

They are examples of deformation without slip, included as non-slip cases while matching force to the cases being distinguished. They keep the learning problem focused on telling deformation apart from impending slip rather than relying on an easy difference in force. The proposal does not specify a particular matching procedure.
So the negatives are not just arbitrary contacts where nothing happens?

Right. The proposal specifically calls for deformation negatives matched for force. They matter because deformation can produce tactile changes even though the target event—impending grasp slip—is absent.
Does including those negatives guarantee a false-positive rate of 5% or less?

No. They are a proposed way to train the distinction, not a performance guarantee. The goal still calls for at least 90% recall, no more than a 5% false-positive rate, and prediction at least 100 milliseconds ahead under its stated evaluation conditions. Those outcomes would have to be demonstrated rather than inferred from the choice of training examples.
How does wear augmentation relate to worn sensors?

Wear augmentation is the proposed training component aimed at making the model less dependent on an unworn sensor condition. It is relevant because performance is required with worn sensors. The proposal does not specify how wear would be represented in the augmentation, and adding augmentation by itself does not establish performance on worn sensors.
Is the 120-ms figure how long a contact must be observed before making a prediction?
No. Here, 120 milliseconds is the proposed forecast horizon: the model is intended to predict slip 120 milliseconds before it occurs. The proposal does not specify an observation-window length.
How does that horizon relate to the at-least-100-millisecond warning requirement?

A correctly timed 120-ms-ahead slip forecast would provide more than the required 100 milliseconds of lead time. But choosing a 120-ms forecast horizon does not, by itself, show that forecasts will be accurate or that the recall and false-positive targets will be met.
Could I call it a 120-ms slip detector?
“120-ms slip forecast” is clearer. “Detector” might suggest recognizing slip once it is occurring, whereas this proposal is about predicting impending slip 120 milliseconds ahead.
Does the proposal say what kind of model to use?

Only that it is a force-conditioned tactile model. No architecture, training objective, or other implementation detail is specified. The defining parts of this proposal are its force conditioning, the shear-drift and strain-recovery signals, the matched-force deformation negatives, wear augmentation, and the 120-ms forecast horizon.
Would it be fair to say the model learns to separate movement-related tactile change from elastic change?

As a broad intuition, yes, provided the wording stays tied to the stated task: distinguishing impending grasp slip from elastic deformation. The proposal does not assert that every instance of either kind of change has a unique signature or that the chosen signals already separate them reliably.
Does this proposal include a claim that it generalizes to unseen materials?

It is directed at the goal that includes unseen materials, but it does not report a generalization result. Whether a model trained this way meets the targets on held-out materials remains an evaluation question.
I also don't want wear augmentation to sound like a substitute for checking worn sensors.

That distinction is important. Wear augmentation is part of the proposed training approach. Meeting the goal on worn sensors is a required outcome; it cannot be concluded merely because wear augmentation was used.
Can we state the proposal in one sentence without making it sound proven?

Propose training a force-conditioned tactile model on shear-drift and strain-recovery signals, using matched-force deformation negatives and wear augmentation, to produce slip forecasts 120 milliseconds ahead.
What is the main distinction that sentence should keep visible?

The forecasts are for impending grasp slip, not for tactile change in general. The matched-force deformation negatives are there because elastic deformation without slip must not be confused with that event, including when the force is comparable.
And none of this says the 120-ms forecasts have already met the recall and false-positive targets?

Correct. It describes how to train a model and what forecast horizon to aim for. It does not report results on recall, false positives, held-out materials, worn sensors, or the force-matched deformation-only contacts.
Can force-conditioned shear-drift and strain-recovery cues distinguish incipient slip from force-matched elastic deformation on worn sensors?

That is the open question. The proposed cues might contain information that separates an emerging slip from deformation without slip, but their ability to do so on worn sensors has not been established here. Matching force makes the distinction more specific: a difference in force alone should not account for the answer.
What does “incipient slip” mean in this question?

It means slip that is beginning or impending, rather than a contact that has merely deformed. The question asks whether the tactile cues can distinguish that slip-related state from elastic deformation that is not slip.
Why mention force conditioning if the contacts are matched for force?

The two serve different roles. Force conditioning means interpreting shear-drift and strain-recovery cues in the context of force. Force matching makes the deformation comparison harder to resolve by force alone. Together, they frame a question about whether those tactile cues remain discriminative when force is comparable.
Does force-matched mean the slip and deformation contacts are identical in every respect except slip?

No. The question specifies matching for force, not identity in every other respect. It also does not define precisely how force matching is performed. The key point is that the comparison should not be answered merely by noticing a force difference.
What are we asking of the shear-drift cue specifically?

Whether information in shear drift, interpreted with force, helps tell incipient slip apart from force-matched elastic deformation. The question does not assume that any particular amount or pattern of drift uniquely indicates slip.
And strain recovery?

Similarly, it asks whether strain-recovery information helps make that distinction. Recovery can be considered as a cue about how deformation changes, but the question does not establish a fixed recovery pattern for either class.
Is the question whether each cue works by itself?

As phrased, it is about force-conditioned shear-drift and strain-recovery cues together. It does not specify that either must succeed independently, nor does it rule out asking separately about their contributions. The central issue is whether the proposed cues can support the distinction under the stated conditions.
Could a contact show elastic deformation while also being close to slipping?

The wording does not require deformation and incipient slip to be mutually exclusive physical processes in every contact. It asks whether the cues distinguish incipient slip from the comparison case of force-matched elastic deformation without slip. Treating any deformation as automatically excluding slip would oversimplify that question.
Why is the worn-sensor condition part of the question rather than an afterthought?

Because the question is specifically whether the distinction can be made on worn sensors. A cue could seem informative in one sensor condition without answering whether it remains informative when the sensor is worn. No particular form or degree of wear is specified here.
Are we assuming wear destroys the cues?
No. Nor are we assuming it leaves them unchanged. The effect relevant to this question is unresolved: can the force-conditioned cues still distinguish the two cases on worn sensors?
If shear drift is visible, would that settle it?

Not on its own. The comparison is with elastic deformation at matched force, so the issue is whether the observed cue separates incipient slip from that alternative, not simply whether a tactile change is visible. Visibility of a cue is different from demonstrated discriminative value.
Likewise, could I take a strain-recovery signal as proof that the contact is deformation-only?

No. A strain-recovery signal is one of the proposed sources of information, not a categorical label. The question leaves open how informative it is when interpreted alongside shear drift and force on a worn sensor.
What would a positive answer to the question actually establish?

It would establish that, under the worn-sensor and force-matched comparison being asked about, the force-conditioned shear-drift and strain-recovery cues can distinguish incipient slip from elastic deformation without slip. The question itself does not provide such a finding or specify a measured level of separation.
And if those cues do not distinguish the cases, does that mean force conditioning has no value at all?

That would be too broad. A failure to distinguish these particular cases on worn sensors would answer this specific question negatively; it would not, by itself, settle every possible use of force conditioning. The question is deliberately narrower than a judgment about all tactile prediction methods.
Does this question claim that wear augmentation has already solved the worn-sensor problem?

No. Wear augmentation is part of the proposed approach, but this question asks whether the relevant cues distinguish the cases on worn sensors. A proposed training component is not evidence that the distinction has been achieved.
Is the force-matched deformation case meant to be a genuine alternative explanation for the tactile signals?

Yes. Elastic deformation without slip can be the relevant alternative to an incipient-slip interpretation. Matching force keeps the question focused on whether shear-drift and strain-recovery cues add distinguishing information, rather than relying on force as an easy separator.
Can we answer the question just from the names of the cues?

No. The names describe the kinds of tactile information under consideration; they do not show how reliably those signals separate the two contact states, especially on worn sensors. Whether they do so is exactly what remains open.
So the question isn't asking whether worn sensors can register any tactile signal at all?

Correct. It asks a more specific thing: whether the force-conditioned shear-drift and strain-recovery cues can discriminate incipient slip from force-matched elastic deformation on worn sensors. Registering a signal alone would not answer whether the two cases can be told apart.
How should I phrase the uncertainty without implying the proposal failed?

You can say: “It remains to be determined whether force-conditioned shear-drift and strain-recovery cues distinguish incipient slip from force-matched elastic deformation on worn sensors.” That states the question without asserting either success or failure.

My hypothesis is that force-conditioned cues can achieve at least 90% recall for slip forecasts 120 milliseconds ahead, with a false-positive rate no higher than 5%, on worn sensors and unseen materials, including force-matched deformation contacts.

That states a testable hypothesis, not an established result. It predicts that the force-conditioned cues will provide 120 milliseconds of advance warning for at least 90% of slips while keeping false positives at or below 5% under the named conditions. Force-matched deformation contacts are especially important non-slip cases for that prediction.
Does this hypothesis answer whether the cues distinguish incipient slip from elastic deformation?

It proposes a positive answer, with numerical performance thresholds and the worn-sensor, unseen-material, and force-matched-deformation conditions made explicit. It does not show that the answer is positive; that remains to be determined.
When I say “120-ms slip recall,” do I mean that a warning can arrive any time within 120 milliseconds after slip?

No. Here it means recall for forecasts made 120 milliseconds ahead of slip. A warning after slip would not be a 120-ms-ahead forecast, and a warning that arrives too late would not satisfy that forecast timing.
Why keep the recall and false-positive figures in the same hypothesis?

They capture both sides of the proposed distinction. At least 90% recall concerns how often impending slips receive the required advance warning. A false-positive rate of no more than 5% concerns how rarely non-slip contacts are incorrectly flagged, including the force-matched deformation contacts. The hypothesis requires both, rather than trading an unrestricted number of false alarms for high recall.
Is the 5% limit saying that at most 5% of predicted slips can be wrong?

No. False-positive rate concerns the proportion of non-slip cases that are incorrectly flagged as slip, not the proportion of slip predictions that are wrong. The hypothesis specifies a false-positive-rate limit of 5% or less.
Does “force-matched deformation” mean that deformation counts as an impending slip if the force matches?

No. It refers to deformation without slip used as a comparison at matched force. The hypothesis is that the cues can still distinguish impending slip from those non-slip deformation cases, rather than interpreting similar force as evidence that both contacts are slipping.
What does the force conditioning contribute to the claim?

It identifies the cues as being interpreted in the context of force. The hypothesis is not that force alone separates the cases: force-matched deformation makes that an inadequate explanation of the proposed distinction. Whether force conditioning actually helps achieve the thresholds is part of what remains unproven.
Am I specifically hypothesizing that the earlier shear-drift and strain-recovery cues meet these targets?

Those are the cues under discussion in the proposed approach. This hypothesis assigns a quantitative expected outcome to the force-conditioned cues, rather than claiming that shear drift or strain recovery has already been shown to work. It also does not say either cue must meet the thresholds on its own.
Why mention worn sensors and unseen materials together?

Both are conditions under which the hypothesis expects the thresholds to hold. It is not limited to familiar materials or an unworn sensor condition. The wording does not specify particular materials, degrees of wear, or a separate numerical result for each condition.
Would successful forecasts on unseen materials alone establish the full hypothesis?

No. The hypothesis also names worn sensors and force-matched deformation contacts, as well as the 120-ms timing, at least 90% recall, and no more than 5% false positives. Evidence limited to unseen materials without the other stated conditions would not establish the whole claim.
Could the false-positive target be checked only on easy non-slip contacts?

That would leave out a condition expressly included in the hypothesis. Force-matched deformation contacts are non-slip cases that need to be accounted for when assessing whether the cues distinguish slip from elastic deformation while meeting the false-positive limit.
Does the hypothesis specify exactly how recall or false-positive rate must be aggregated across the named conditions?

No. It states the thresholds and the conditions—worn sensors, unseen materials, and force-matched deformation—but does not prescribe a detailed aggregation or reporting scheme. That detail should not be read into the hypothesis.
Can I say the 120-ms forecast is better than the original at-least-100-ms warning requirement?

As a timing target, 120 milliseconds ahead is earlier than 100 milliseconds ahead. But the hypothesis does not establish that the earlier forecasts have been achieved, or that the recall and false-positive thresholds are met. It is an expectation to evaluate, not a performance result.
If a model attains 90% recall but has a 6% false-positive rate, would that satisfy the hypothesis?

No. The hypothesis requires both at least 90% recall for the 120-ms forecasts and a false-positive rate of no more than 5%. A 6% false-positive rate would exceed that stated limit, regardless of whether the recall threshold was reached.
And if the false-positive rate is below 5% but recall is below 90%?
That would also fall short of the hypothesis. Keeping false positives low does not replace the requirement to forecast at least 90% of slips at the specified 120-ms horizon.
Should I phrase it as a guarantee that wear augmentation will make the cues robust?

No. Wear augmentation is part of the proposed training approach, whereas this hypothesis concerns the performance expected on worn sensors. Neither the augmentation nor the hypothesis itself guarantees that performance.
How can I keep the wording precise and visibly hypothetical?

You could say: “We hypothesize that force-conditioned shear-drift and strain-recovery cues will forecast slip 120 milliseconds ahead with at least 90% recall and no more than a 5% false-positive rate on worn sensors and unseen materials, including force-matched deformation-only contacts.” That retains the proposed outcome without presenting it as observed.
Is the central uncertainty still whether the cues separate impending slip from deformation, rather than merely respond to tactile changes?

Yes. The hypothesis predicts that the separation will be strong enough to meet the stated 120-ms recall and false-positive thresholds under the named conditions. Responding to tactile change in general would not by itself establish that force-matched deformation is being distinguished from impending slip.
How should we plan to investigate whether the cues distinguish incipient slip from force-matched elastic deformation on worn sensors?

The plan is to collect force-matched slip and deformation trials, train a wear-augmented cue model, and then calibrate and test its 120-ms slip forecasts on held-out materials and worn sensors. Those are proposed steps, not experiments already completed or evidence that the distinction has been achieved.
Why start with both slip and deformation trials?

The question is not just whether the model can recognize something associated with slip. It is whether it can distinguish impending slip from elastic deformation without slip. Collecting both kinds of trials gives the proposed model examples of the target event and the comparison case.
What work does the force matching do in those trials?

It makes the slip and deformation comparison more focused. If the cases differed readily in force, a model might appear to distinguish them by relying on that difference. Force-matched trials are intended to test the distinction when force is comparable. The plan does not specify a particular matching procedure.
Are the deformation trials supposed to be mislabeled as slips to make training harder?

No. Deformation without slip is the non-slip comparison case. Its value is that it may involve tactile change without the event the forecasts are meant to predict. The plan is to collect those trials alongside slip trials, not to call deformation a slip.
Does collecting force-matched trials mean every other condition in a pair is identical?

No. The plan says force-matched; it does not say the trials are identical in all other respects or prescribe how they are paired. The stated purpose is to keep a force difference from being an easy explanation for distinguishing slip from deformation.
What is meant by a cue model here?

It refers to the tactile model being developed around the cues under discussion: force-conditioned shear-drift and strain-recovery information. In this plan, the model is to be trained with wear augmentation. The plan does not specify its architecture or claim that the cues will succeed.
Is wear augmentation the same thing as testing on worn sensors?

No. Wear augmentation is part of the proposed training step; testing on worn sensors is a separate evaluation step. Augmenting training does not, by itself, establish that forecasts work when sensors are worn.
Do we know exactly what the wear augmentation will look like?

Not from this plan. It calls for a wear-augmented cue model but does not define the augmentation method or a degree of wear. Those details should remain unspecified rather than being presented as decisions already made.
Why calibrate the forecasts instead of going straight from training to testing?

Calibration is an explicit step in the plan between training and testing. In general, it concerns how a model's forecast outputs are interpreted as predictions. The plan does not say which calibration method to use or report a calibrated result.
Does calibration mean we can simply adjust the answer until the test meets the desired numbers?

No. Calibration is a planned step, not a license to treat test outcomes as established or to redefine the target. The plan still calls for testing the 120-ms forecasts on held-out materials and worn sensors. It does not specify a procedure for choosing calibration settings.
What exactly is being forecast 120 milliseconds ahead?

Slip. The intended forecast is an advance indication of impending grasp slip 120 milliseconds before it occurs, not a label assigned 120 milliseconds after it occurs. The plan does not specify how long a tactile observation must be before making that forecast.
Could we describe the testing as ordinary slip detection?

That would obscure the timing requirement. The planned test is of 120-ms slip forecasts, so it needs to address whether the prediction comes ahead of slip, as well as whether slip and deformation are distinguished.
Why are the materials held out?

The plan calls for testing on held-out materials so that the evaluation addresses materials outside those used to develop the model. It is a way to examine the proposed distinction across unseen materials, rather than only in familiar material conditions. No particular materials are specified.
Are held-out materials and worn sensors interchangeable test conditions?

No. They address different aspects of the stated challenge. Held-out materials concern material generalization; worn sensors concern performance under sensor wear. The plan names both for testing and does not say that testing one substitutes for testing the other.
Does the plan specify whether the held-out-material and worn-sensor tests are separate or combined?

It specifies testing 120-ms forecasts on held-out materials and worn sensors, but not the exact arrangement of those conditions. We should preserve both conditions without inventing a particular grouping or evaluation protocol.
Where does the force-matched deformation comparison show up after collection?

It remains central to what the forecasts need to distinguish. Collecting force-matched slip and deformation trials supplies the comparison for training the cue model; testing the forecasts must still speak to the question of slip versus deformation. The plan does not give an exact composition for the test cases.
Could a test that includes slip trials but no deformation cases answer the question?

It could say something about slip forecasts, but it would not by itself resolve whether the cues distinguish incipient slip from force-matched elastic deformation. That comparison is the reason the plan calls for both kinds of trials.
Does the plan promise that the model will meet the 90% recall and 5% false-positive targets?

No. Those are performance targets for the slip-prediction goal, not results produced by writing down a collection, training, calibration, and testing plan. The planned tests would provide evidence about whether the forecasts meet the required timing and performance conditions.
What would be premature to say after only collecting the trials?

It would be premature to say that the cues distinguish slip from deformation, that wear augmentation works, or that 120-ms forecasts meet any performance target. Collection is the first proposed step; training, calibration, and testing are still part of the plan.
What if the model is trained but not yet tested on worn sensors?
Then the planned worn-sensor test would still be outstanding. Training a wear-augmented model is not equivalent to demonstrating its forecasting performance on worn sensors.
Can the sequence be stated without suggesting that we have already run it?

Yes: collect force-matched slip and deformation trials; train a wear-augmented cue model; then calibrate and test its 120-ms slip forecasts on held-out materials and worn sensors. Using prospective wording keeps the sequence distinct from a report of completed work.
Is the point of the plan to evaluate the cues rather than assume their meaning in advance?

Yes. The plan puts the proposed cues into a model and tests its advance forecasts against slip and deformation cases under the named material and sensor conditions. It does not assume that shear drift or strain recovery is, on its own, a definitive sign of slip.
So even if the model issues a forecast 120 milliseconds before a contact changes, that isn't automatically a correct slip forecast?

Correct. The forecast has to concern impending slip, not tactile change in general. A force-matched contact that deforms without slipping is part of why the plan calls for a discriminating test rather than simply checking whether the model responds early to change.
Let's run WearSlip-120 leave-material-and-wear-out testing. What exactly should this activity measure?

It should measure recall for slip forecasts made 120 milliseconds ahead, and the false-positive rate on force-matched deformation-only contacts. The leave-material-and-wear-out setting puts those measurements under the material and sensor-wear conditions the test is meant to examine. Running the test does not, by itself, imply any particular result.
Why is it called leave-material-and-wear-out testing?

The name identifies the evaluation setting: material and wear conditions are left out for testing, so the forecasts are examined beyond the conditions used to develop the model. The activity does not specify the exact partitions, the number of materials, or the wear conditions involved.
Does WearSlip-120 refer to the 120-millisecond warning?

WearSlip-120 is the name of this test, and the activity explicitly measures 120-ms slip forecasts. The relevant timing is advance prediction: whether slip is forecast 120 milliseconds before it occurs, not whether it is recognized 120 milliseconds afterward.
What counts toward the slip-recall measurement?

The measurement concerns how often actual slips receive the specified 120-ms-ahead forecast. A response only after slip begins would not demonstrate recall at that forecast horizon. The activity does not spell out a more detailed counting protocol.
Why measure false positives specifically on deformation-only contacts?

They are non-slip contacts that can nevertheless involve tactile deformation. Measuring false positives on them directly probes whether the forecasts mistake elastic deformation for impending slip, rather than merely reacting to a changing tactile signal.
And those deformation-only contacts must be force-matched?

Yes. The activity specifically calls for the false-positive rate on force-matched deformation-only contacts. Matching force makes the non-slip comparison pertinent to the question of whether the tactile cues distinguish slip from deformation when force is comparable.
If one of those contacts is flagged as about to slip, how is that treated?

For this measurement, it is a false positive: the contact is deformation-only, not an impending slip. The false-positive rate expresses how often such non-slip contacts are incorrectly flagged. The activity does not state what that rate will be.
Does the test measure false-positive rate across every possible kind of non-slip contact?

The activity names force-matched deformation-only contacts for that measurement. A rate measured on those contacts should be described as such, rather than silently generalized to every possible non-slip contact.
Would high slip recall alone tell us the cues distinguish slip from deformation?

No. A predictor could forecast many slips while also incorrectly flagging deformation-only contacts. WearSlip-120 measures both 120-ms slip recall and false positives on the force-matched deformation-only comparison so that the two sides of the distinction remain visible.
The hypothesis gives thresholds of at least 90% recall and at most 5% false positives. Is WearSlip-120 the test of those figures?

Yes. Its specified measurements are the ones needed to evaluate that hypothesis at the 120-ms horizon under the named conditions. The thresholds are criteria to compare against the measurements, not outcomes that can be assumed before the test reports them.
If the test shows 90% recall, can I say the whole hypothesis is supported without looking at deformation contacts?

No. You would also need the false-positive measurement on the force-matched deformation-only contacts, and the result would need to be understood in the leave-material-and-wear-out setting. Slip recall alone addresses only one part of the hypothesis.
Is a forecast made shortly before slip, but not 120 milliseconds ahead, interchangeable with a 120-ms forecast?

No. The activity specifically measures 120-ms slip recall. A forecast at a different, shorter lead time cannot simply be counted as satisfying that measurement. The timing condition is part of what WearSlip-120 tests.
What does leaving wear out add beyond testing with worn sensors?

It makes the wear condition part of the holdout setting rather than merely a condition the model may have encountered during development. The activity calls this leave-material-and-wear-out testing; it does not define the precise way wear conditions are represented or divided.
Should we assume the test uses a particular level of sensor wear?
No. Worn sensors and a wear-out testing condition are part of the activity, but no specific wear level is supplied. Naming one would add a test detail that has not been stated.
Likewise, do we have a list of the materials being left out?

No. The test is specified as leave-material-and-wear-out, but the materials and their allocation are not given. The point to preserve is that performance is measured under the material holdout condition, without inventing a particular list.
Does running this test mean the model has already been calibrated and its performance established?

No performance is established by the activity description. WearSlip-120 is the testing activity for the 120-ms forecasts; it supplies no measured recall or false-positive rate. It also does not provide calibration details.
Can I describe the force-matched deformation cases as the negative side of the evaluation?

Yes. They are non-slip cases on which a slip forecast would be a false alarm. Calling them the negative comparison keeps clear why their false-positive rate is measured separately from recall on actual slips.
Is the test asking whether the tactile cues exist on worn sensors, or whether forecasts based on them are discriminative?

The stated measurements address forecast performance: 120-ms recall for slips and false positives on force-matched deformation-only contacts in the leave-material-and-wear-out setting. Merely observing a tactile cue on a worn sensor would not answer whether the forecasts distinguish the two kinds of contact.
